title: How Internet Censorship Works
summary: Josh and Chuck explore internet censorship in its many forms: parental web filters (blacklists, keyword blocking, Net Nanny, CYBERsitter) versus firewalls; employer censorship such as blocking Facebook at work; government censorship, including the Open Net Initiative's categories, China's suppression of the "Under the Dome" pollution documentary and salt rumors after Fukushima, India's suppression of a documentary on a public transport rape case, Iran's proposed "Halal Internet," and the fracturing of the Internet into separate national internets as described by Eric Schmidt and Jared Cohen. They cover Reporters Without Borders' list of offending countries, Cuba's slow internet, net neutrality and common carrier status, opposition from the ACLU to COPA and SOPA, and internet kill switches including DHS Standard Operating Procedure 303 and the 2011 BART cell phone shutdown in San Francisco. The episode closes with listener mail about a honeymoon flight.
topics: Reporters Without Borders press freedom list

segments.title: Opening banter and corrections
segments.summary: Hosts joke about being banned in China and about past episodes, then Josh corrects an earlier claim about poisonous spiders and bites to dogs. They introduce internet censorship as the topic, crediting a TechStuff article.

segments.title: Parental web filters and software
segments.summary: Discussion of why parents may filter the web for children, with software like Net Nanny and CYBERsitter. Web filters use blacklists of domain names or keyword scanning, with a joke about a clubhouse computer blocking a male puberty article.

segments.title: Firewalls versus web filters
segments.summary: The hosts distinguish a firewall, which protects a computer or network from incoming threats, from a web filter, which restricts outgoing access to websites. Critics note keyword filters lack context, as with a chicken breast recipe.

segments.title: Workplace censorship and Facebook
segments.summary: Employers block sites at work, and Facebook is described as the most blocked site, partly due to time wasting and hostile work environment concerns. Hosts also apologize for trolls invading the show's Facebook page.

segments.title: Government censorship and the Open Net Initiative
segments.summary: Government censorship is introduced as the most contentious level, with the Open Net Initiative's political, social and other categories. Examples include China's removal of the Under the Dome documentary and India's clumsy removal of a documentary about a transit rape case.

segments.title: China, salt rumors, and Iran's Halal Internet
segments.summary: China is described as a prolific censor that targets calls for collective action. China quashed a 2011 salt rumor after Fukushima. Social censorship is discussed, including Iran's proposed Halal Internet.

segments.title: Splinter internet and Eric Schmidt's vision
segments.summary: Discussion of the Foreign Affairs style article by Eric Schmidt and Jared Cohen envisioning separate national internets, internationalized domain names, virtual passports, and the possibility of bypassing the domain naming system.

segments.title: Reporters Without Borders list and Cuba
segments.summary: Reporters Without Borders lists offending countries including Belarus, China, Cuba, Iran, Myanmar, Saudi Arabia, North Korea, Syria, Tunisia, Turkmenistan, Vietnam and Uzbekistan. Cuba's slow internet and the historically government-run internet cafes are covered.

segments.title: Net neutrality and common carrier status
segments.summary: The hosts explain net neutrality, the FCC's reclassification of ISPs as common carriers, and why throttling speeds could effectively censor slow-loading sites and squeeze out startups.

segments.title: ACLU, COPA and SOPA opposition
segments.summary: The ACLU fought the Children's Online Protection Act in court, and the Stop Online Piracy Act is described as threatening sites that link to pirated material. Critics saw both as tools for government censorship.

segments.title: Sponsor break
segments.summary: Brief sponsor mention that includes a joke about the World Book Encyclopedia.

segments.title: Internet kill switches and SOP 303
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the so-called internet kill switch, DHS Standard Operating Procedure 303, its origins in the 2005 London bombings, the 2011 BART cell phone shutdown in San Francisco, and Egypt's shutdown during 2011 protests. A pending EPIC lawsuit seeks transparency.

segments.title: Listener mail: honeymoon flight
segments.summary: A listener from Seattle describes a noisy Russian triplets flight to Maui and a drunk passenger on the return flight, and thanks the hosts for helping them stay calm.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts give social media and email contact info and sign off.
